hints: Focus on what each axis means, electronegativity on the y-axis and first ionisation energy on the x-axis, and recall how each changes across Period 3.
Remember electronegativity rises steadily from Na to Si, so Na must be lowest and Si highest vertically, which already rules out two diagrams.
Recall the dip in first ionisation energy from Mg to Al due to the 3p electron, so Al must sit to the left of Mg horizontally even though it is above Mg vertically.
walkthrough:
**Order the electronegativity vertically**

Think of electronegativity as pull on bonding electrons. Across Na to Si, nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so pull increases steadily.

Order from low to high: $$\text{Na} < \text{Mg} < \text{Al} < \text{Si}$$

**Order the first ionisation energy horizontally**

First ionisation energy is energy to remove the outer electron: $$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + e^{-}$$
Across the period it generally increases, but there is a dip at Al. Mg has configuration $[\text{Ne}]3s^2$ while Al is $[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1$. The 3p electron is further out and shielded, so easier to remove.

**Combine both orders**

So on the x-axis from left to right: $$\text{Na (lowest)} < \text{Al} < \text{Mg} < \text{Si (highest)}$$
This is the key trap. Vertically Al is above Mg, but horizontally Al is to the left of Mg. Only one diagram shows this crossover pattern with Si top right and Na bottom left.

options.A: Shows a perfect straight line increase for both properties. It correctly orders electronegativity Na < Mg < Al < Si, but it wrongly orders ionisation energy as Na < Mg < Al < Si. It misses the well known dip from Mg to Al caused by moving from 3s to 3p.
options.B: Correct on both axes. Vertically, electronegativity increases Na < Mg < Al < Si. Horizontally, first ionisation energy follows Na < Al < Mg < Si, with Al to the left of Mg and Si furthest right. This matches the 3s to 3p dip.
options.C: Reverses the electronegativity trend. It puts Na highest and Si lowest on the y-axis, which is opposite to the true periodic trend where electronegativity increases across the period as nuclear charge increases.
options.D: Also reverses electronegativity, putting Na at the top and Si at the bottom. It also puts Al below Mg vertically, which is wrong because Al (1.61) is more electronegative than Mg (1.31).
